questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page gives 0 downgrades in 36 recorded S&P actions on a stable outlook (0%). I treat 0% as a floor, not a forecast: records are incomplete, and France is a fiscally stressed minority government in a thin sample. The market price (11% for a Moody's or S&P downgrade by 30 Nov) is a cross-check only.

factors.text: Reference class: S&P has never downgraded one of the six tracked EU sovereigns from a stable outlook in the recorded history. Agencies usually move the outlook first, and the question counts an outlook change alone as NO.

Moody's already affirmed Aa3 negative on 23 Oct 2026, so no fresh peer cut is adding pressure. The 11% market price covers Moody's or S&P, and Moody's has already reviewed, so it is mostly S&P; that is above the 0% base rate and suggests some tail risk is priced.

France's spread to Germany is widening (96.7 bp in September from 81.5 bp in August, monthly averages). The 2027 budget is in doubt (about half odds of passage by 31 Dec) and the government is a minority. This keeps a downgrade tail alive, mainly through an outlook cut or a censure shock before 27 Nov.

questions.what_would_change_view: A successful censure motion or a rejected first reading of PLF 2027 before 27 Nov would raise my view. So would a higher 2026 deficit estimate, or S&P moving the outlook to negative before the review. A calm budget passage with no censure would lower it.
questions.most_likely_wrong: The consensus and the base rate both treat S&P as slow and sequential. A political collapse in November could make S&P skip the outlook step and cut directly, as France's widening spread and its minority government suggest it could.
questions.title: S&P review of France, 27 Nov 2026

questions.base_rate_used: The page gives 19 of 21 budgets promulgated by 31 December (90.5%) across 2006-2026. That class is a poor fit for a minority parliament. Since the government lost its majority in June 2022, only 2023 (49.3) was promulgated by year-end. The 2025 and 2026 budgets each needed a special law in December and were adopted later. I start from roughly one in four for the recent subset, not 90%, and weigh it against the markets at about half.

factors.text: The long-run base rate is high, and a 49.3 on the joint-committee text, as in December 2022, can still deliver promulgation by 31 December. Kalshi puts 49.3 use at 66%, and the Polymarket and Kalshi budget markets sit near half (51% and 49%).

Under the minority government, the 2025 budget ended in a special law and the 2026 budget was adopted only in January and February 2026. The spring 2027 presidential election gives parties little reason to share the blame for a budget. The special-law path was widely expected in the previous two cycles.

Article 47 ordinance has never been used under the Fifth Republic, so it adds little to YES even though it counts. The day-70 deadline is 10 December, but a joint-committee failure in mid-December usually leads to a special law. Use of 49.3 also exposes the government to censure, which would mean NO.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if the Socialists or Les Républicains signal they will not vote a censure motion, or if a joint-committee agreement appears by mid-December. I would move down if the first-reading revenue part is rejected, if a censure motion gathers Socialist votes, or if the government openly prepares a special law.
questions.most_likely_wrong: The crowd at about half may be right: a non-censure deal with the Socialists, as in the 2026 budget but earlier, could produce a 49.3 adoption before Christmas. The three-year special-law pattern could also be a feature of those specific years, not a lasting regime.
questions.title: France 2027 budget and the Article 47 deadline

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page gives no computed probability for an RN win. It only says the final-poll leader won 4 of 4 run-offs, with an RMS poll error of 5.78 pp on final polls, and that error is larger six months out. So I start from the market price: Le Pen 43% and Bardella 2.1% on Polymarket, Le Pen 46% and Bardella 1.3% on Kalshi, which is roughly 45% combined.

factors.text: The markets price RN at roughly 45% six months out, with a large poll error of 5.78 pp on final polls and more before that. Long-dated markets that split the opposition across many candidates can overstate the single frontrunner's chance. RN has also lost both recent run-offs.

The crowd has just made a large shared error in Brazil. Lula won after odds gave Flávio Bolsonaro 80%, and outlets describe the result as bucking a regional shift to the right. That is a warning against taking a right-populist narrative at face value.

The market shows no sign that Le Pen's eligibility case is a risk, since she still trades at 43%. The base rate also says the final-poll leader won 4 of 4 run-offs, and RN is a strong first-round favourite. This holds the number near the market and stops me cutting further. The poll-versus-market gap gauge shows no lead, so I put little weight on any signal from it.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up on a ruling confirming Le Pen can run, or on second-round polls showing RN ahead of the strongest centre-right candidate. I would move down if the centre-right consolidates behind one candidate, or if the eligibility case removes Le Pen and Bardella polls clearly worse. The rating and budget events this autumn would change my view only if a censure vote or downgrade visibly boosts RN.
questions.most_likely_wrong: I may be wrong to shade below the market. The anti-RN barrier may have weakened, so RN could win a run-off against a fragmented opposition. The market's 43% for Le Pen may then be about right or too low.
questions.title: France 2027 presidential election

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate; em-macro records no Brazilian fiscal-target revisions. I start from the page's context, that Brazil cut its own primary target in July 2015 and April 2024, and treat that as a loose reference class. Both cuts came with the April budget-guidelines cycle. That points to roughly even odds, so I start near 50%.

factors.text: Timing favours YES. Past target cuts came with the April budget-guidelines bill, after the 31 March cutoff. The new term only starts on 5 Jan 2027, and the 2027 budget vote is in December. A formal bill to change the target or LC 200 before 31 March is therefore less likely than a de facto loosening through exclusions or one-offs, which still counts as YES.

The market is already penalising loosening risk. The Brazil 10y proxy and the DI Jan-29 proxy are about 2 percentage points above a week ago, after Lula's run-off win. That gives the government a reason to avoid an early formal rewrite and to keep the framework on paper.

The Focus median for the 2027 primary balance is -0.3% of GDP against a +0.5% target, so the survey already expects a miss. The government has cut its own target before, in 2015 and 2024. Pressure to change the target or exclude spending is real. This survey series is untested, so I give it little weight.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move toward NO on a PEC, PLP or PLN to change the target or LC 200 appearing early, on ministers publicly questioning the 0.5% target, or on the Focus 2027 primary-balance median falling further. I would move toward YES on the 2027 budget passing in December without new exclusions, on a finance minister who keeps the framework being named, and on the March bimonthly report freezing spending.
questions.most_likely_wrong: The government sends a bill, or a PEC counted as changing the spending limits, in January to March 2027 to loosen the framework while it holds a fresh mandate. Or the March bimonthly report itself proposes a change. The market repricing suggests investors may be reading this correctly.
questions.title: Brazil 2027: fiscal-framework credibility

questions.base_rate_used: The page has no computed base rate for the two-thirds threshold. Its reference class is only that the final-poll leader won Mexico's midterms 3 of 3 (2009, 2015, 2021), with a poll error of 4.12 pp. In 2021 the governing coalition kept its majority but lost two-thirds. I start near even odds for keeping two-thirds, because the coalition holds it now but midterms usually cost the governing side seats. There is no direct market on the two-thirds question.

factors.text: Markets give Morena about 89% to win the most seats. That says the coalition is the clear favourite, but the price is not a view on two-thirds. It leaves a modest chance of a large loss and says little about the 334-seat line.

The 2024 case showed that a poll margin between two candidates cannot capture the supermajority outcome. Seat allocation and the rules on coalition over-representation matter more than the headline vote. Consensus that treats the seat count as simply following the vote is likely wrong in both directions.

Midterms without a presidential race usually cost the governing side seats. In 2021 the coalition lost two-thirds. Reaching 334 of 500 needs strong vote share plus favourable over-representation, which is a high bar. The survey-dispersion gauge for Mexico is flagged as having no lead, so the poll signals deserve little weight.

questions.what_would_change_view: Polls putting the coalition above 55% of the vote, or an INE ruling that keeps or widens coalition over-representation, would raise my view. Coalition polling below 45%, or an alliance of the opposition parties in key districts, would lower it. A direct market on the two-thirds threshold would also help, since none exists now.
questions.most_likely_wrong: I may be underweighting the coalition's overall dominance and high presidential approval, which would make two-thirds the default outcome. Equally, I may be underweighting the usual midterm erosion and the legal uncertainty over over-representation, which would make two-thirds the exception. The range is wide with 219 days to go.
questions.title: Mexico midterms, 6 Jun 2027

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate: this is the agreement's first review cycle, and em-macro has no trade-agreement events. I start from the market price instead, the nearest available anchor: Polymarket gives 8% that USMCA is extended in 2026, and Kalshi gives 24% for a trilateral revised deal in 2026. Both are related but not identical markets.

factors.text: Markets price a 2026 extension at only 8%. The 2026 review window has largely passed without an extension, so annual reviews are now the default under art. 34.7. This leaves a modest chance that all three parties confirm in writing by 1 July 2027.

A trilateral revised deal is priced at 24% on thin volume. That shows some chance of a negotiated outcome that includes a written extension. Official US-Mexico trade contacts continue, for example the Peñasquito remediation, so the process is not broken.

US trade policy shows leverage-driven, unscheduled behaviour, such as the USTR statement on the EU détente. All three parties confirming in writing, including the US, needs the US to give up that leverage. Withdrawal or bilateral splits remain live tail risks.

questions.what_would_change_view: A USTR report or statement recommending extension, US tariffs on Mexican goods cut below 10%, or a trilateral text announced would raise my view. A Federal Register withdrawal notice, or a US proposal for separate US-Mexico and US-Canada texts, would lower it sharply.
questions.most_likely_wrong: A broad deal could be struck before July 2027 with all three confirming extension in writing, as the thin Kalshi price hints. The crowd may also be too pessimistic, treating annual reviews as the stable equilibrium when the US may prefer a clean extension once concessions are secured.
questions.title: USMCA annual review, 1 Jul 2027
